title: Real object, or camera fault?
task: Say which explanation fits all four readings on the board.
scene: Three survey pictures show the same faint dot in three different places. The background stars have not moved. A telescope on another mountain has just found the dot too.
question: The dot moved and the stars did not. What does that tell you about the dot?
takeaway: Something real moves against the stars, and a camera fault stays where the camera put it.
why: A real object moves against the sky. A camera fault moves with the camera. That is the test, and every reading here uses it. The dot is round in all three pictures, so it is not a cosmic ray, which hits once and hits sharp.

choices: A real object out in the Solar System
A cosmic ray hitting the camera
A hot pixel on the chip
The pictures were lined up wrong
choiceMechanisms: A real object shifts against the stars and lands on a new part of the chip each time.
A charged particle leaves one sharp mark, in one picture only.
One spot on the chip reads bright every time that spot is read.
A bad line-up drags many stars the same way at once.
rebuttals: A cosmic ray hits once and looks sharp. This dot is round in all three pictures, and it keeps moving.
A hot pixel is bright wherever that pixel sits. This dot lands somewhere new each time.
A bad line-up would drag many stars along. Here the stars hold still and one dot does not.
text.headline: The survey software flags a faint dot that moves near the ecliptic.

title: Check it before you send it
task: Put the four steps in the order they have to be done.
scene: Forty thousand stars, two satellite streaks and a bad column of pixels share the pictures with the moving dot. The camera's calibration is the check against known stars that says what its numbers mean. The discovery notice goes out at dawn.
takeaway: A claim is worth sending out once somebody else can test it.
why: Each step throws out a different kind of mistake. Cleaning removes what the camera itself adds. Matching removes the satellites, the known faults and the objects already on the list. Measuring turns a picture into numbers, with a range that says how sure you are.

rebuttals: Cleaning comes first. Positions measured off a dirty picture are wrong, and no later step fixes that.
Matching comes second, or you measure a satellite or a bad pixel very carefully.
Measuring comes third, with how sure you are. A position with no range on it fits nothing.
The prediction comes last. It is the step that lets somebody else prove you wrong.
cards: Remove the camera's own marks, and solve exactly where it was pointing.
Check every dot against the star and satellite lists.
Measure where it is and how bright, with a range.
Post a predicted position, so another observatory can look and check.

title: How fast is it moving?
task: Turn the shift between two pictures into a rate the next telescope can use.
scene: The dot shifted between two pictures taken twenty minutes apart. The next telescope has to be told where to point. Nobody has turned that shift into a rate yet.
question: About how fast is it moving, in arcseconds per hour?
takeaway: Two pictures and a clock turn movement into a rate you can point with.
why: Angular speed is a rate, so the units have to match before anything is divided. Six tenths of an arcsecond a minute is thirty-six arcseconds an hour, because an hour holds sixty minutes. This is not how fast the rock really flies.

estimate.prompt: The dot moves twelve arcseconds in twenty minutes. Before anyone points a telescope, that has to become a rate per hour.
estimate.question: About how fast is it moving, in arcseconds per hour?
estimate.relationship: Rate = how far it moved ÷ how long it took. Minutes become hours by multiplying by sixty.
estimate.explanation: The sixty in the template is the minutes in an hour, so the time has to be in minutes. Use the same gap in seconds and the answer comes out sixty times too small.
estimate.solution: Twelve ÷ twenty is six tenths of an arcsecond a minute, so about thirty-six arcseconds an hour.

title: Why do the positions disagree?
task: Make the defense call before the next observation window closes.
scene: One wide camera's positions bend away from the orbit near one edge of its chip. The clock checks out. A second telescope, watching the same object, shows nothing odd.
question: The misses appear at one edge of one camera's chip, and nowhere else. Where is the fault?
takeaway: An error that follows the equipment is telling you about the equipment.
why: The reference stars are the control. They do not move, so anything that shifts them belongs to the equipment. Here they miss by more toward one edge of the chip, and the asteroid misses the same way. That is a pattern in chip position, not in the sky.

choices: The camera's map from chip to sky is out of date
The asteroid is really speeding up
The recorded times are wrong
The star list is wrong everywhere
choiceMechanisms: A stale chip-to-sky map pushes the stars and the asteroid the same way near the edge.
A real force in space moves the asteroid and nothing else.
A wrong exposure time shifts moving objects and leaves fixed stars where they belong.
A bad star list is wrong in the same way at every telescope and across the whole field.
rebuttals: A real push acts on the asteroid alone. The stars would stay where they belong, and here they do not.
A clock error moves the asteroid and leaves the stars right. Both are off here, and the clock checks out.
A bad star list would show up at the second telescope too, and all across the field rather than at one edge.
text.headline: One camera's follow-up positions curve away from the orbit. A second telescope agrees with the orbit.

equations.about: what a push does to something heavy

title: Build the arc
task: Put the four steps in the order they have to be done.
scene: Six observatories have sent positions. Two used a different time standard, and one sent no pointing solution at all. Together they cover four hours.
takeaway: A path is tested by where the object turns up next, not by how well it fits the past.
why: A short arc fits many paths at once. They agree about where the object has been and disagree about where it goes. Time is what pulls them apart. Wait a few nights and paths that matched the same measurements spread out across the sky. So the real test is a prediction.

rebuttals: Same map and same clock first. Two time standards in one fit hide inside the answer afterwards.
A rough path second. You need something to measure the misses against.
The misses third. Scatter is noise, but a pattern that follows one station is a fault.
The prediction last. It is the only step the sky can prove wrong.
cards: Put every measurement on the same map and the same clock.
Fit a first rough path across the sky.
Look at what the fit misses, and why.
Say where it will be tomorrow, closely enough to point.

title: Why waiting helps
task: Make the defense call before the next observation window closes.
scene: Four hours of spare time on a two-metre telescope, and the object sets soon after dusk. Two possible paths fit tonight's measurements equally well. The same patch of sky comes back in six nights.
question: Two paths fit tonight equally well. What makes them easier to tell apart?
takeaway: Two paths that agree today drift apart with time, so a later look separates them better than a sharper look now.
why: Two paths through the same point tonight are heading slightly different ways. Tonight they sit on top of each other. No camera can split them, however sharp it is. Six nights later that small difference has become a real gap in the sky. One picture then does what ten pictures tonight cannot.
answerText: Time. Let both paths run for six nights and they end up in visibly different places.

choices: Waiting, and looking again in six nights
Taking a sharper picture tonight
Taking many pictures tonight in a row
Using a bigger telescope tonight
rebuttals: A sharper picture of tonight still has both paths in the same place.
Ten pictures of the same moment is one moment, ten times.
A bigger telescope sees fainter, and it cannot see the future.
text.setup: Two possible paths fit tonight's measurements equally well.

title: Read the risk correctly
task: Move and narrow the cloud of paths until all of it clears Earth.
scene: The best-guess path misses Earth, and the cloud of possible paths around it still touches the impact line. Dr. Marco Rossi, the orbit lead, wants one sentence before the briefing.
question: What has to change before the whole cloud of paths clears Earth?
takeaway: Risk lives in the whole spread, not in the middle of it.
why: An orbit is a spread of possible paths, not a dot. Fixing a known bias slides the whole spread sideways. It does not make the spread any thinner. Better measurements do make it thinner, but they do not choose where the middle sits. The call needs both.
answerText: Neither move is enough on its own. Do both. The near edge then sits at 4.5 − 3.2 = 1.3 Earth radii, and the whole cloud clears Earth.

cloud.hint: The center is the nominal miss and the width is the current uncertainty. Try the two authored improvements separately before combining them; clearance requires the whole displayed band to remain outside the Earth-limb boundary.

actions.label: Correct the catalog bias in the nominal orbit

shape.hint: The center is the nominal miss and the width is the current uncertainty. Try the two authored improvements separately before combining them; clearance requires the whole displayed band to remain outside the Earth-limb boundary.

title: What does an impact chance mean?
task: Match each risk statement to what it really says.
scene: Dr. Isabel Garcia, the survey and response lead, has a computer cloud of possible future paths. A few cross Earth and most do not. The public number is a chance, not a prediction that one exact future has been chosen.
takeaway: An impact probability is the share of still-possible paths that hit Earth. New measurements can move or shrink that set.
why: The computer keeps many paths that fit the measurements. Some hit Earth and others miss. The fraction that hit becomes the current chance. A new observation can remove many possible paths, so the chance can rise or fall without the asteroid suddenly changing direction.
answerText: Treat the number as a statement about the current set of possible paths, not as a countdown to a guaranteed impact.

text.setup: Drag each statement to the correct interpretation.
choices: A chance, not a promise
More data could change it
A spread of paths, not one line
Better measurements narrowed it
rebuttals: Probability describes how many still-allowed paths hit.
New measurements can remove or shift allowed paths.
The data still allow many paths, not one exact future.
A changed probability usually means our knowledge changed, not that the rock jumped.
scenarios: A small share of allowed paths hit Earth
A new telescope night is scheduled
The orbit is still uncertain
The chance drops after new measurements

title: Point where the answers disagree
task: Make the defense call before the next observation window closes.
scene: The best guess misses by four Earth radii, and about one path in six hundred still hits. Next Tuesday the two sets of paths sit eight arcseconds apart. After that they close up again.
question: A thin set of paths still hits Earth. Where do you point next week?
takeaway: The best measurement is the one whose result the rival answers would disagree about.
why: A measurement only teaches you something where the rival answers disagree. Here that is one night. On Tuesday the hitting paths and the missing paths sit eight arcseconds apart. Any follow-up telescope can tell those apart. Before and after, both sets predict the same spot.

choices: Where the hitting paths and the missing paths point to different places.
Wherever the object is brightest and easiest to measure.
At the same patch of sky again, to improve the camera calibration.
Nowhere new — run the same measurements through another orbit program.
rebuttals: The brightest night is the easiest measurement and the least useful one. Every path already agrees about where it will be.
Better calibration helps every measurement a little, and tells the two sets apart not at all.
Another program checks the arithmetic rather than the sky. Worth doing, and it adds no measurement.

title: What makes it look bright?
task: Match each change to what it does to the brightness we measure.
scene: The object was bright enough for the survey to spot it, and people across the room are reading that one number as a size. Four things that change brightness are on the board.
takeaway: A bright asteroid is not always a big one.
why: Brightness is four things multiplied together, which is why size and surface get tangled. A bigger rock catches more sunlight. A better reflector sends back more of what lands on it. Distance from the Sun sets how much sunlight arrives at all.

choices: More light comes back, because there is more surface catching sunlight.
More of the sunlight landing on it is sent back.
Less sunlight arrives to be sent back at all.
What does come back is spread thinner before it gets here.
rebuttals: A bigger rock catches more sunlight and sends more back. This is the one everybody assumes is the whole story.
A shinier surface returns more of what lands on it, at the same size. This is what makes brightness ambiguous.
Further from the Sun means less sunlight arrives in the first place.
Further from us means what comes back is spread thinner by the time it arrives.
scenarios: The rock is bigger across.
The surface reflects better.
The rock is further from the Sun.
The rock is further from us.
columns: What that does to the brightness

title: Same brightness, two different rocks
task: Match each clue to what it can and cannot tell you.
scene: Dr. Tola Adebayo, the physical-characterization lead, shows two asteroid models that look equally bright. One is small and shiny. One is larger and dark. Brightness alone cannot tell you which model is right.
takeaway: Brightness can be explained by size or by how reflective the surface is. A second kind of measurement is needed to separate them.
why: A small shiny rock can reflect as much light as a bigger dark rock. That means one brightness measurement has two possible explanations. Heat or another independent measurement can break the tie and give a better size.
answerText: Do not choose a size from brightness alone. Use a second measurement, such as thermal infrared, to break the tie.

text.setup: Drag each clue to the conclusion it earns.
choices: Could be small and shiny
Could be large and dark
Brightness alone cannot decide
Use a second measurement
rebuttals: A reflective surface can look bright without being large.
A dark surface may need to be larger to look equally bright.
The same brightness fits more than one size-and-surface combination.
A heat measurement gives new information that does not depend on reflected light in the same way.
scenarios: A bright object with a very reflective surface
A bright object with a dark surface
Only one visible-light brightness measurement
A thermal-infrared observation is available

title: Settle the size
task: Fit the reflected light, then use the heat reading to settle the size and the surface.
scene: Reflected light alone puts the rock somewhere between one hundred and twenty and six hundred metres across. The heat team now has an infrared reading from the same night.
question: Which width and which surface fit the reflected light and the heat at once?
takeaway: A tie between two answers is broken by a measurement that depends on them differently.
why: Reflected light depends on size and surface together, so many pairs fit it equally well. That is a tie, not a noisy measurement, and measuring the same light more carefully will never break it. Heat depends on the two the other way round.
answerText: Reflected light allows a whole family of pairs. The heat reading crosses that family near one hundred and eighty metres across, with a surface reflecting about 0.44 of the light that lands. The glow also puts the surface near seventeen degrees Celsius.

degeneracy.hint: First move diameter and albedo until the reflected-light proxy is matched; several combinations work. Then use the thermal spectrum and flux, which respond to absorbed and emitted energy, and satisfy both constraints at once.

shape.hint: First move diameter and albedo until the reflected-light proxy is matched; several combinations work. Then use the thermal spectrum and flux, which respond to absorbed and emitted energy, and satisfy both constraints at once.

title: Whose dip is it?
task: Open what each spectrum depends on, keep the ones that stand alone, and name what the rest share.
scene: A wide dip has turned up in the spectrum, which is the rock's brightness measured colour by colour. It would change what the rock is made of. A star, a second look through more air, and a spectrum taken from space are all on the board.
question: Does the dip belong to the rock, or to the air it was seen through?
takeaway: Measurements that share one path do not check each other.
why: Three views can agree because all three looked through the same air. A plain star has no dip of its own, and this one shows the dip too. Lower in the sky the light came through more air, and the dip got deeper.
answerText: The dip belongs to the air. The rock, the plain star and the low-in-the-sky look were all seen through it. The telescope above the air shows no dip at all.

trace.hint: Do not count how many plots show the dip. Open what each one looked through, keep the ones that took a different path, and then name what the rest have in common.

channels.label: A plain star, from the ground
channels.reading: the same dip, at the same colour

channels.label: The rock again, lower in the sky
The rock, from a telescope above the air

shape.hint: Do not count how many plots show the dip. Open what each one looked through, keep the ones that took a different path, and then name what the rest have in common.

title: From light to what it is made of
task: Put the four steps in the order they have to be done.
scene: The spectrum has two dips and a slope. Three different mineral mixes match it just as well as each other. A draft notice naming one of them is already being typed.
takeaway: A good answer about what something is made of keeps the other answers that still fit.
why: Cleaning has to come first, because the Sun, the air and the instrument are all inside what the camera recorded. A dip found before they are removed may belong to any of them. Reflectance is then a property of the rock. Only after that is it worth asking which features hold up.

rebuttals: Cleaning first. The Sun's own colours and the air's are in the recording, and a dip found before they go may be theirs.
Reflectance second. It is the part that belongs to the rock rather than to the night.
Features and models third. Weathering, grain size and viewing angle all copy a change in minerals.
The alternatives last. A class with nothing beside it claims more than the data can hold.
cards: Take out what the Sun, the air and the instrument each added.
Measure how much light the surface sends back, colour by colour.
Take the features that hold up, and try several minerals.
Report what fits, and what would settle the rest.

title: Make the claim stronger
task: Make the defense call before the next observation window closes.
scene: The draft notice names what the rock is made of. One spectrum backs it. Next door the deflection team is sizing a spacecraft from the weight that class implies.
question: The rock turns as it goes. What does watching it at other angles add?
takeaway: Ask for evidence that could disagree with you, not for a firmer label.
why: A firmer claim needs evidence that could disagree with the one you have. More colours reach features this spectrum cannot see at all, so whole families of minerals can be ruled out. Another look tonight, taken the same way, repeats the same mistakes.

choices: Look at more colours than this spectrum covers.
Watch it at other angles and other points in its spin.
Add a measurement of the surface texture, taken a different way.
Nothing more — publish the class and mention the doubt.
rebuttals: Other angles and spin phases test whether the surface is the same all over. That matters once the list is short, not before.
Texture measured another way checks whichever class survives. On its own it does not shorten the list.
Publishing with a note attached is the same claim in smaller type, and a spacecraft gets sized from it anyway.

equations.about: what a push does to something heavy

equations.e: change in position = change in speed × time
equations.about: why a deflection works better early

title: What does radar measure?
task: Match each thing we want to know to the radar reading that measures it.
scene: The radar room has its first clean run of echoes. Delay, pitch shift and echo width are up on one screen. The orbit team is waiting to hear which reading to use.
takeaway: Each radar reading measures one thing, and none of them measures all of it.
why: Radar pulls apart what a picture leaves tangled, and each reading pulls apart something different. The delay of the echo is a time, and with a known speed a time is a distance. The spread in pitch is the range of speeds across the rock, which is spin.

choices: Time the echo. Radio has a known speed, so time gives distance.
Measure the spread in pitch. One side comes, one goes.
Read when each part of the echo returns. Later means further.
Build pictures across a full turn, and fit them together.
rebuttals: A distance is a speed multiplied by a time, and the delay of the echo is the time radar hands you.
Spin shows up as a spread of speeds across the rock, and a spread of speeds is a spread of pitches.
Where along the line an echo came from is carried by when it arrives back.
A whole shape needs the rock seen from many sides, which is what one full turn gives you.
scenarios: How far away it is.
How fast it spins.
How much of the rock sits at each depth.
Its whole shape, and the spin that carries it round.

title: How far away, from the echo?
task: Turn the echo time into a distance the orbit team can use.
scene: The dish sent a pulse, and the echo came back four seconds later. The characterisation team needs a distance before the next run starts.
question: About how far away is the object?
takeaway: An echo becomes a distance once you know the speed and the time.
why: Radar hands you a time, and a time becomes a distance as soon as the speed is known. Radio travels three hundred thousand kilometres each second. Four seconds is one million two hundred thousand kilometres of travelling. The pulse went out and came back, so the rock sits half that away.

estimate.prompt: The pulse left the dish and the echo came back four seconds later. Counting in thousands of kilometres, radio covers 300 of them every second.
estimate.question: About how far away is the object, in thousands of kilometres?
estimate.relationship: Distance = speed × time ÷ two, because the pulse went there and back.
estimate.explanation: Forget to halve it and the answer is twice too big. That is how far the pulse travelled, not how far away the rock is.
estimate.solution: Four seconds at 300 thousand kilometres a second is 1,200, and half of that is 600 thousand kilometres out.
labels: 300 (thousands of kilometres radio covers each second)

title: What this pass does to the next one
task: Make the defense call before the next observation window closes.
scene: Radar has pinned this pass at 2.4 Earth radii and the room starts to relax. Then the return solution flashes up on the board: eleven years.
question: Radar has settled this pass. What has to be worked out before anybody calls the object safe?
takeaway: A close pass rewrites the path it happens on, so safety is a claim about the passes after it.
why: A measured miss settles this pass and not the next one. Passing a few Earth radii out lets Earth's gravity pull on the rock and change its speed and its direction.

choices: Carry this pass forward, and check the later ones.
Use this miss as the final answer, since it is leaving.
Pin down the size first, and judge safety from that.
Take fresh measurements after the pass, and stop there.
rebuttals: A measured miss settles this pass and says nothing about the path the pass creates.
Size is worth knowing, and it does not say where the rock will be in eleven years.
A fresh arc is needed and is not enough. Without carrying the orbit through the pass there is nothing to compare it with.

title: Build the impact meter
task: Match each asteroid card to whether the impact energy goes up a little, a lot, or not at all.
scene: Dr. Rohan Banerjee, the impact physics lead, gives you four asteroid cards. You are not calculating giant numbers. Your job is to learn which changes make a collision more powerful.
question: Which changes make an impact more energetic?
takeaway: A heavier asteroid carries more impact energy, and a faster asteroid carries much more.
why: Mass matters because more moving material carries more energy. Speed matters even more because the speed is used twice in the energy rule. For a first pass, the key is the pattern: heavier means more, and much faster means much more.
answerText: More mass raises the energy. More speed raises it even more strongly. Changing only the label or colour does not change the impact energy.

choices: Energy rises
Energy rises a lot
Energy stays about the same
Need more information
rebuttals: More moving mass means more impact energy.
A large speed increase has a very strong effect on impact energy.
A surface colour by itself does not set the collision energy.
Sometimes a card is missing either mass or speed, so you cannot compare fairly.

scenarios.label: Same mass and speed, different colour
One card has no speed measurement

title: The speed jumped — what changes first?
task: Choose the briefing item that must be upgraded immediately.
scene: A new tracking run says the asteroid would arrive much faster than the earlier estimate. Dr. Rohan Banerjee, the impact physics lead, freezes the briefing before it goes public.
question: What should the team change first?
takeaway: Impact speed strongly changes how much damage a moving object can do, so a big speed change forces a new consequence estimate.
why: A faster moving object carries more impact energy, and speed has a strong effect. A large change in the arrival speed is therefore not a small correction. The consequence estimate must be rerun before the team repeats the old damage range.
answerText: Recalculate the consequence range before reusing the old briefing; the faster arrival can make the impact much more energetic.

choices: Recalculate the consequence range
Keep the old damage range and change only the time
Ignore it because the mass did not change
Announce the worst case immediately
rebuttals: A big speed change can strongly change impact energy and damage.
The old damage range depended on the old speed.
Mass is not the only thing that sets impact energy.
The team should update the evidence before jumping to the worst case.

title: Which measurement is worth the most?
task: Make the defense call before the next observation window closes.
scene: The range of harm runs from one region to a whole continent. Every part of that range comes from a measurement. There is time to improve one of them.
question: The range of consequences is enormous. Which measurement narrows it most?
takeaway: Improve the measurement that carries the most error into the answer, not the one that is easiest to repeat.
why: Weight comes from volume, and volume is the width multiplied in three times over. So an error in the width arrives at the energy three times as wide as it started. Density goes in once.

choices: The width, from heat measurements or from radar.
The density, from what the rock is made of.
The speed and the angle it arrives at.
None of them — report the worst case and plan for that.
rebuttals: Density goes in once and is genuinely uncertain. Worth improving, and worth about a third as much.
Speed goes in twice, and it is already the best known of the three, so there is least left to win.
Reporting only the worst case settles nothing. It also spends public attention on a number nobody can defend.

title: How much does the push move it?
task: Work the craft's push into a change in the rock's speed.
scene: The deflection lab is sizing a spacecraft. It knows the craft's weight and how fast it would close, and the rock's weight to within a factor of a few.
question: How far will the nudge have moved the rock by the time it arrives?
takeaway: The same push moves a heavier thing less, in exact proportion.
why: The push is tiny. A craft weighing ten tonnes hits a rock weighing eight billion, so the rock's speed changes by about fifteen millimetres a second — walking pace divided by two hundred. What makes it matter is that the rock keeps that speed, second after second, for eight years.

estimate.prompt: The push speeds the rock sideways by fifteen millimetres a second, which works out at about 475 kilometres in a year. The encounter is eight years away.
estimate.question: How far will the rock have moved by then?
estimate.relationship: Distance moved = how far it shifts in one year × the number of years.
estimate.explanation: The millimetres a second are the same fact in a smaller unit, not a second thing to multiply by. Do this nudge one year out instead of eight and it buys an eighth as much room.
estimate.solution: About 475 kilometres in a year, for eight years, is about 3,800 kilometres.
labels: 475 km (how far the nudge moves it in a year)

equations.about: what a push does to something heavy

equations.e: change in position = change in speed × time
equations.about: why a deflection works better early

title: What makes a deflection work?
task: Match each item on the board to what it does to the outcome.
scene: The impactor plan is up on the mission board. Beside it sit the weight estimate and the tracking plan. The director wants it all sorted before the review.
takeaway: A deflection is an experiment, and the thing it changes is the orbit.
why: A deflection has four separate parts, and only one of them is the collision. The push that lands depends on the craft's weight and closing speed. What that push does depends on the rock's weight. Material thrown off the surface adds more push, by an amount nobody can predict yet.

choices: The same change in speed moves it further.
The size of the change cannot be predicted well.
The push that lands is bigger or smaller than planned.
It measures what really changed, not what was promised.
rebuttals: More warning multiplies the same small change into more distance. It is the cheapest thing in the whole problem.
The rock's weight divides the push, so an uncertain weight is an uncertain result, in direct proportion.
Material thrown off the surface carries momentum away and adds to the push, by a factor nobody can predict.
Tracking afterwards measures the change that happened rather than the one that was expected.
scenarios: More years of warning.
The rock's weight is not well known.
Nobody knows how much material will be thrown off.
Tracking after the impact.
columns: What it does to the outcome

equations.about: what a push does to something heavy

equations.e: change in position = change in speed × time
equations.about: why a deflection works better early

title: Say what you expect, then measure it
task: Lock a predicted range, run the impact, then spend the tracking to find out what happened.
scene: The impactor has hit and the control room is cheering. Nobody has measured the orbit yet. One tracking campaign is left in the budget.
question: Did the measured change in the orbit match what was predicted before the impact?
takeaway: An action is not finished until somebody measures what it did.
why: The momentum sum gives a smallest change of about one and a half centimetres a second. Material thrown off the surface can add to that. So the prediction has to be a range, not one number. A hit proves the craft arrived. It does not measure the new orbit.
answerText: The hit works. The job is finished only once tracking measures the new orbit. Here the measured change is 2.1 centimetres a second. That sits inside the predicted 1.5 to 4.5, so the model that sized the craft holds up.

verify.hint: The momentum calculation gives the lower-bound scale, but ejecta can change the result. Lock the expected range before impact. After the hit, do not stop at a successful collision—buy the tracking measurement and compare it with what you predicted.

shape.hint: The momentum calculation gives the lower-bound scale, but ejecta can change the result. Lock the expected range before impact. After the hit, do not stop at a successful collision—buy the tracking measurement and compare it with what you predicted.

title: Match what you do to what you know
task: Match each state of the evidence to what it justifies doing.
scene: The regional team is round one table. The wall shows the newest corridor, the likely damage area and the time left. Today they choose what to do.
takeaway: You can prepare in stages without ever claiming to be certain.
why: What you do depends on three things: how bad it would be, how long you have, and whether you could undo it. Years in hand means there is still time to learn more, so watch and prepare cheaply. A rising chance is worth real preparation, as long as it can be undone.

choices: Keep watching, and prepare in ways that waste nothing.
Move supplies in and plan the routes, because both can be undone.
Order people to move, under emergency powers.
Stand down in public, and say why.
rebuttals: A tiny chance with years in hand buys the cheapest thing there is. Keep watching, and prepare in ways that cost nothing.
A rising chance over a corridor that holds still is worth real supplies, because supplies can be moved back out.
With days left, being able to undo it stops being the deciding thing. What it would cost takes over.
A falling chance is stood down out loud, with the reason. Dropping it quietly is how the next warning gets ignored.
scenarios: A tiny chance, with years still to run.
A rising chance, and the corridor holding still.
A high chance, with days left.
The chance falls after a decisive measurement.

title: How many people is that share?
task: Turn the chance and the population into a number the office can plan against.
scene: The emergency office needs a number to plan against. It has the people living inside the corridor. It has today's chance of impact. And it has a form to fill in.
question: How many people does that share come to?
takeaway: A small share of a very large number is still a number somebody has to plan for.
why: This number is a share, not a headcount. Half of one per cent of nine million people is forty-five thousand. Nobody expects exactly that many people to move. Either the rock misses and nobody moves, or it hits and far more than that do.

estimate.prompt: Nine million people live inside the corridor. Today's chance of impact is half of one per cent.
estimate.question: How many people does that share come to?
estimate.relationship: Part = the whole × the share, once the share is written as a decimal.
estimate.explanation: Half of one per cent is 0.005, not 0.5. Put the percentage straight in without converting it and the answer is a hundred times too big.
estimate.solution: Nine million × 0.005 is forty-five thousand people.
labels: 5 (people in every thousand, at today's chance)
2,000 (thousands of people in the biggest city there)

title: Prepare without panic
task: Set the threshold for each stage before the updates arrive, then release the stream.
scene: Five orbit updates are queued. Planners can still prepare without moving anybody. Both planning and supplies take time, and the thresholds have to be set before the stream starts.
question: Which thresholds still leave enough time for planning and for moving supplies?
takeaway: A rule written before the numbers arrive is the only rule the numbers cannot bend.
why: A threshold is a decision made before the next number lands. Preparation takes time, so an action that is right can still be useless if it starts too late. Setting the rule first also stops every new number being judged by a new standard.
answerText: Set planning near 0.25 per cent and supplies near 0.75 per cent, before the stream runs. Both then fire with time still in hand. Waiting for the last update at 1.4 per cent leaves none.

trigger.hint: Write both action thresholds before releasing the next orbit updates. The first action needs two days of lead time; the second needs one. A rule that triggers after its operational lead time is gone does not count as a successful plan.

shape.hint: Write both action thresholds before releasing the next orbit updates. The first action needs two days of lead time; the second needs one. A rule that triggers after its operational lead time is gone does not count as a successful plan.

title: What each claim has earned
task: Match each claim to what the evidence under it justifies doing.
scene: The board has to publish one account of an eight-year campaign. The four claims in front of it rest on very different evidence. Whoever runs the next one will read it.
takeaway: Different claims in one document have earned different amounts of confidence.
why: These four claims are in four different states, and giving them one level of confidence is how a report stops being trusted. A shift that somebody else has confirmed can be accepted. An edge nobody has pinned down is a reason to keep watching, not a reason to quote the middle.

choices: Accept it, and keep checking.
Keep observing, and do not treat the middle as the whole answer.
Update them before anybody uses them.
Fund the searching and the readiness for the long run.
rebuttals: An orbit shift somebody else has confirmed is the strongest claim here. Accept it, with checking going on.
An edge nobody has pinned down is not a safe middle. Treating it as one is the mistake this whole campaign was about.
Plans built on an old corridor are worse than no plans, because somebody will pick them up and use them.
Gaps in the search have nothing to do with this rock and everything to do with the next one.
scenarios: Tracking shows the orbit shift, and somebody else confirms it.
The best guess is safe, and the edges are not pinned down.
The plans are ready, and they use an old corridor.
No threat from this rock, and the sky is still not covered.

title: Signed is not checked
task: Spend the two checks on the signed claims that most need measuring.
scene: Two checks are left before the record goes public tonight. Every claim in it is signed. Some of them would change the conclusion if they were wrong.
question: Which signed claims have to be checked before the record goes out?
takeaway: A signature records a decision. It does not measure a thing.
why: A record can be trusted when somebody else can rebuild what was measured and how. A signature says a person approved it. It does not say the thing is true. So the checks go to claims that matter and that nobody has confirmed another way.
answerText: Spend both checks on the measured push and on the size. Both matter, and neither has been confirmed by anybody else. The path has already been worked out twice.

attest.hint: Every card is signed, and a signature is only a record. You can check two of them properly. Spend the checks where a wrong claim would change what the record says, and where nobody has confirmed it another way.

claims.label: The path of the rock has been worked out twice
claims.evidence: a second team, using their own software and their own measurements, got the same path

claims.label: The push we gave it was measured, and by how much
claims.evidence: nobody has refitted the before-and-after positions since the night it happened

claims.label: How big the rock is, and how sure we are
claims.evidence: the size rests on one heat measurement that nobody has redone

claims.label: The words of the public notice have been approved
claims.evidence: the press office signed off the wording this afternoon

shape.hint: Every card is signed, and a signature is only a record. You can check two of them properly. Spend the checks where a wrong claim would change what the record says, and where nobody has confirmed it another way.

title: What survives the success
task: Make the defense call before the next observation window closes.
scene: The threat is gone, and so is most of the budget. The search still misses parts of the sky, and two follow-up sites lose their funding at the end of the year.
question: The campaign budget ends with this review. What survives it?
takeaway: The lasting defence is a system that can find, learn, decide and act again.
why: Warning time is what every later choice gets bought with. Finding a rock earlier gives more nights to check the orbit. It gives time to measure the size and what it is made of. It makes a small push worth giving, because years turn a push into distance.

choices: Keep the search and the quick follow-up, and the links.
Move the money to studying rocks and testing nudges.
Move the money to civil readiness, and wait for warnings.
Stop spending. The catalogue and the automatic alerts have it covered.
rebuttals: Studying rocks and testing deflections are both worth having, and they need an object found early enough for any of it to matter.
Readiness turns a warning into action. It cannot make a warning if nothing finds the rock in the first place.
This campaign is the evidence against that. The gaps, the viewing angles and the follow-up were all short.

equations.about: what a push does to something heavy
